title: Processing Fluency and Aesthetic Pleasure: Is Beauty in the Perceiver's Processing Experience?
authors: Reber, R., Schwarz, N., Winkielman, P.
key_findings: Core proposal: the more fluently a perceiver processes an object, the more positive the aesthetic response; beauty is 'objectified', not objective.

Four assumptions: objects differ in fluency (symmetry, figure-ground contrast, goodness of form, prototypicality, repetition, priming); fluency is hedonically marked (positive); people use the feeling as information unless its value is questioned; impact is moderated by expectation and attribution.

Fluency is discounted when people attribute the feeling to an irrelevant source (e.g., background music); fluency that comes as a surprise (expected hard, turns out easy) gives the strongest pleasure, a reading of 'unity in variety'.
Inverted-U for complexity is explained as two opposing mechanisms (salience of the fluency source vs loss of fluency).

Experts prefer more complex/asymmetric stimuli; the authors propose training raises fluency for complex stimuli and experts apply explicit norms of taste, sometimes down-rating simple stimuli despite their ease.
Simplicity is not the same as ease: redundant, contextual patterns can be easier than sparse ones; actual ease must be tested.
practical_applications: Make the main read easy (contrast, clear figure-ground, familiar layout) and put the challenge in meaning, not in decoding.
An 'aha' (looks complex, resolves simply) is the strongest fluency payoff: good for story-carousel final slides.
limitations: Theory/review paper; the authors call the evidence on complexity, expertise and valence 'sparse and sometimes contradictory'.
Mostly lab stimuli (abstract patterns, words); fluency effects on real artworks and ads are smaller and context-dependent.

title: Prototypes Are Attractive Because They Are Easy on the Mind
authors: Winkielman, P., Halberstadt, J., Fazendeiro, T., Catty, S.
key_findings: With random-dot and geometric patterns, prototypicality predicted both categorisation speed (fluency) and attractiveness.
Fluency partially mediated the prototypicality-attractiveness link; some effect of prototypicality remained when fluency was controlled.
Facial EMG: prepared (fluent) prototypes produced quick extra activity over the cheek (smile) muscle, i.e., a genuine mild positive affect, not only a cold judgement.
practical_applications: A recognisable category look (a clear 'eyewear shop' or 'story card' prototype) earns an immediate small liking bonus; deviate from it deliberately, not randomly.
limitations: Abstract lab patterns; small effects; does not test meaningful commercial images.
Beauty-in-averageness for faces may also have other causes (the authors say fluency explains part, not all).

title: Neuroaesthetics
authors: Chatterjee, A., Vartanian, O.
key_findings: Aesthetic experience emerges from interaction of three systems (the 'aesthetic triad'): sensory-motor, emotion-valuation, meaning-knowledge; the systems are not always equally weighted.

Context changes valuation: abstract images labelled 'museum' were rated more attractive than when labelled 'computer-generated', with more medial OFC/vmPFC activity; 'art status', titles and authenticity (original vs copy) modulate responses.
Aesthetic pleasure may reflect 'liking' without 'wanting' (Berridge), a neural reading of Kant's disinterested interest.
Default mode network (DMN) involvement in the most moving artworks is cited from Vessel et al. 2012.

Limits: meaning of individual artworks is fluid and historically contingent; the biggest challenge is reverse inference from brain location to mental process, which should generate hypotheses, not confirm them.
practical_applications: Framing (caption, label, 'handmade', 'by our optician') is part of the aesthetic object; plan it as deliberately as the image.
Treat brain-region claims in marketing ('this lights up the reward centre') as unproven.
limitations: Short review (2014); field has since grown and critiques of small-sample fMRI apply.
Context-label study is cited, not re-analysed here.

title: Move me, astonish me... delight my eyes and brain: The Vienna Integrated Model of top-down and bottom-up processes in Art Perception (VIMAP) and corresponding affective, evaluative, and neurophysiological correlates
authors: Pelowski, M., Markey, P. S., Forster, M., Gerger, G., Leder, H.
key_findings: Per abstract: VIMAP integrates artwork-driven (bottom-up) processing with top-down mechanisms to explain why the same artwork produces very different responses across people.
Per Van Geert & Wagemans 2020: in VIMAP, order and complexity are detected in perceptual analysis and further processed in implicit memory integration.
Per Pizzolante et al. 2024: Pelowski's models frame transformation as expectation-artwork discrepancy that, when resolved, yields insight/epiphany.
practical_applications: Plan for multiple outcomes of one image (facile liking, confusion, rejection, insight) instead of one 'correct' reaction.
limitations: Full text not read; stage details and outcome names unverified here.
Large theoretical model; many links remain to be tested.

title: 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design
authors: Hekkert, P., Snelders, D., van Wieringen, P. C. W.
key_findings: Per a CogSci summary (secondary): three studies with consumer products (sanders, telephones, teakettles, cars, phones); typicality and novelty were negatively correlated but each positively predicted preference, suppressing each other's effect.
Typicality and novelty jointly explained about 56% of preference variance in Study 3; central tendency (objective typicality) gave about 60%.
Experts showed weaker typicality-novelty suppression; the hypothesis that experts rely more on novelty was not supported.
Linked to Loewy's MAYA principle (Most Advanced, Yet Acceptable).
practical_applications: New looks should keep a clear category anchor (recognisable layout, product shape) while adding one novel element.
limitations: Original article not read; numbers come from a third-party summary (which itself has one internal inconsistency).
An apparel study reported no negative typicality-novelty correlation (per search summary), so the pattern is category-dependent.

title: Liking versus Complexity: Decomposing the Inverted U-curve
authors: Güçlütürk, Y., Jacobs, R. H. A. H., van Lier, R.
key_findings: 30 participants rated 144 computer-generated grayscale patterns for liking and complexity; objective complexity = compressed file size (r = .946 with perceived complexity).
Two clusters: 20 people liked simpler patterns (r = -.79 with complexity), 10 liked complex patterns (r = .87).
Averaging the two opposite linear functions produced the group-level inverted U; a two-cluster model fit better than a quadratic model.
Both clusters perceived complexity the same way; they differed in liking, not perception.
practical_applications: Do not aim for 'medium complexity for everyone'; choose complexity per audience segment and test.
File size of a compressed PNG/JPEG is a cheap proxy for visual complexity when comparing variants.
limitations: Small, young sample; post hoc clustering; abstract grayscale stimuli only; 1-second exposures.

title: Order, Complexity, and Aesthetic Appreciation
authors: Van Geert, E., Wagemans, J.
key_findings: Complexity = quantity and variety of information; order = its structure and organisation; following Arnheim, the authors treat them as antagonistic but complementary.
Complexity-liking findings are mixed: inverted U, positive linear (snowflakes, textures) and even U-shaped (solid objects) relations are reported.
Fractal dimension preference typically around D 1.3-1.5 with subgroup differences; Fourier slope about -2 typical of natural scenes and Western graphic art.
Symmetry is usually preferred, but slight asymmetry can be preferred (e.g., Mondrian comparisons); explicit beauty ratings of asymmetry rise with art expertise.

Individual differences: Openness relates to preference for complexity; art training generally relates to preferring complexity; visual working memory capacity predicts preferred complexity; preference for harmony correlates across colour, shape, space and music (Palmer & Griscom 2013).
Authors' view: individuals differ in their preferred balance between order and complexity.
practical_applications: Add order (grid, repetition, alignment, limited palette) when a frame must carry many elements; add variety when an ordered frame feels dead.
Treat complexity preference as audience-specific; order effects are more stable.
limitations: Narrative review (not a meta-analysis), visual modality focus; postprint version read.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: framing credited to Arnheim; open copy is the 2018 accepted manuscript (DOI 10.1037/aca0000224).

title: Visual Complexity and Beauty Appreciation: Explaining the Divergence of Results
authors: Nadal, M., Munar, E., Marty, G., Cela-Conde, C. J.
key_findings: Per search summary and citing papers: divergent complexity-beauty results stem from how studies define and manipulate complexity.
Complexity has at least three dimensions: amount/variety of elements, their organisation, and asymmetry, each relating differently to beauty ratings.
practical_applications: When critiquing 'too busy', say which kind: too many elements, poor organisation, or imbalance.
limitations: Full text not read; details and effect sizes unverified.

title: Back to the inverted-U for music preference: A review of the literature
authors: Chmiel, A., Schubert, E.
key_findings: Per abstract summary: of 57 music-preference studies, 50 (87.7%) were classed compatible with an overarching (segmented) inverted-U, 5 mixed, 2 incompatible.
Authors urge caution in dismissing the inverted-U, while acknowledging problems with Berlyne's arousal theory itself.
A citing paper reports a stricter count (Wundt effects found in only 15 of 57), showing classification dependence.
practical_applications: For music beds and pacing, moderate familiarity/complexity is a reasonable default, but verify with the audience.
limitations: Full text not read; 'compatible' is a lenient category; music domain, not visual.

title: Perceptual and Physiological Responses to Jackson Pollock's Fractals
authors: Taylor, R. P., Spehar, B., Van Donkelaar, P., Hagerhall, C. M.
key_findings: Across natural scenes, computer fractals and Pollock paintings, viewers on average preferred mid-range fractal dimension D about 1.3-1.5 (220-participant study cited).
Skin conductance (24 participants) showed the smallest stress rise for D = 1.4 patterns; EEG (32 participants) showed largest frontal alpha changes at D about 1.3.
Gaze paths are themselves fractal (D about 1.4-1.5), proposed link to foraging-like search.
Pollock's own work rose to D about 1.7, above typical viewer preference.
practical_applications: Backgrounds with natural, moderately rough self-similar texture (clouds, foliage, soft wood grain) are a defensible calm-but-alive choice behind products; avoid both flat dead fields and dense high-D noise behind text.
limitations: Review largely of the authors' own programme; small physiological samples (6-32); fMRI preliminary; D alone does not capture complexity; Van Geert & Wagemans note subgroup differences (inverted-U, positive, negative).

title: Implicit and Explicit Evaluation of Visual Symmetry as a Function of Art Expertise
authors: Weichselbaum, H., Leder, H., Ansorge, U.
key_findings: 79 students (psychology and art history), 80 abstract patterns; symmetrical patterns rated more beautiful (est. means 4.24 vs 2.83 on 1-7).
Implicit (IAT) symmetry-positive association (D = 0.55) did not vary with art expertise.
Explicit ratings of asymmetrical patterns rose with expertise, though experts still rated symmetry higher overall.
practical_applications: Symmetry is a safe default for broad audiences (product hero shots, logos); asymmetry reads as 'designed/artistic' mainly to trained viewers.
limitations: Abstract patterns, lab setting, student sample, custom expertise questionnaire, balance not controlled; correlational.

title: The brain on art: intense aesthetic experience activates the default mode network
authors: Vessel, E. A., Starr, G. G., Rubin, N.
key_findings: 16 observers rated 109 paintings 1-4 for 'how strongly does this move you'.
For the most moving works (rating 4), anterior medial prefrontal cortex (a DMN hub) was not suppressed as it was for 1-3 ratings; PCC, hippocampus, substantia nigra also responded more.
Inter-observer agreement on which paintings moved them was very low (mean pairwise r = .13).
practical_applications: The strongest responses are personal (self-relevant) and idiosyncratic: aim content at a specific audience's lives rather than generic 'beauty'.
limitations: Small fMRI sample (16), typical of the replicability problems described by Turner et al. 2018; no physiological arousal measure.

title: Stronger shared taste for natural aesthetic domains than for artifacts of human culture
authors: Vessel, E. A., Maurer, N., Denker, A. H., Starr, G. G.
key_findings: Per search summary: agreement between observers was high for faces and natural landscapes, low for architecture and artworks.
A second experiment found higher agreement for landscapes than exterior architecture with no reliability difference.
Authors propose natural categories are more uniformly behaviourally relevant, while artifact taste depends on individual experience.
practical_applications: Nature imagery and faces are the 'safer' shared-taste elements; stylised design choices split audiences more.
limitations: Full text blocked (403); numbers not verified here.

title: Aesthetics
authors: Brielmann, A. A., Pelli, D. G.
key_findings: Per press summaries: beauty may be an intense form of ordinary pleasure; beauty and pleasure ratings rise together nearly linearly.
Average features (symmetry, roundness) raise beauty on average, but individual taste differences are large (about half the variance in face attractiveness attributed to personal taste).
practical_applications: Average-based design rules set a floor, not a ceiling; personal relevance drives the top end.
limitations: Only press/secondary coverage read; primer not read.

title: What is interesting? Exploring the appraisal structure of interest
authors: Silvia, P. J.
key_findings: Per search summary: interest rests on two appraisals, novelty-complexity and coping potential (ability to understand it).
Four in-vivo experiments supported this; appraisals predicted interest beyond curiosity/openness traits, and did not predict enjoyment.
practical_applications: Make something new AND give the viewer a handle to understand it (caption, familiar character, clear cue): novelty without coping = confusion.
limitations: Full text not read; a dissertation reports inconsistent coping-potential effects.

title: Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion
authors: Keltner, D., Haidt, J.
key_findings: Prototype of awe: perceived vastness (physical or social size) plus need for accommodation (experience does not fit current mental structures).

Five flavouring appraisals: threat, beauty, exceptional ability, virtue, supernatural causality; e.g., vastness without accommodation = deference, accommodation without vastness = surprise; ability without vastness = admiration; virtue = elevation.
Art that is easily graspable may entertain but rarely induces awe; obscurity and challenge raise accommodation (Burke).
Authors state the approach was developed 'in the absence of empirical evidence'.
practical_applications: Awe shots need scale cues (tiny figure vs vast landscape/sky) plus something not instantly understood; a pretty sunset alone gives beauty, not awe.
limitations: Conceptual paper; later empirical work (e.g., Yaden 2019 scale) builds on it.

title: The development of the Awe Experience Scale (AWE-S): A multifactorial measure for a complex emotion
authors: Yaden, D. B., et al.
key_findings: Per search summary: six factors - altered time perception, self-diminishment, connectedness, perceived vastness, physical sensations, need for accommodation; structure confirmed in a second sample (N = 636).
Japanese adaptation reportedly kept the six-factor structure.
practical_applications: Checklist for an 'awe' beat: slowed time (hold/slow motion), small self (scale), connection, vastness, bodily cue (chills), something to make sense of.
limitations: Full text not read; journal/DOI not confirmed in this session (listed as 'et al.' to avoid guessing co-authors).

title: Towards a Psychological Construct of Being Moved
authors: Menninghaus, W., et al.
key_findings: Three German-language studies (N = 228, 1,683, 901).
Moving episodes mostly involve relationship or critical life events (death, birth, marriage, separation, reunion); sadness (43%) and joy (27%) most often co-reported.
Being moved is a mixed emotion, especially for fiction (positive and negative affect nearly equal); high intensity but low-to-mid arousal; felt as warm, soft, elevating.
Highest appraisals: compatibility with social norms and self-ideals; low appraisal of own causation (observer stance).
practical_applications: Moving story beats come from bonds being tested, lost or restored, watched from a witness position; keep arousal calm (slow pacing, soft sound).
limitations: Self-report, German students only, no physiology; Study 1 scale formatting error.

title: Kama Muta: Conceptualizing and Measuring the Experience Often Labelled Being Moved Across 19 Nations and 15 Languages
authors: Zickfeld, J. H., Schubert, T. W., Seibt, B., ... Fiske, A. P.
key_findings: 19 countries, 15 languages, N = 3,542; KAMMUS scale covering appraisal, valence, sensations, motivation, labels.
Kama muta is a positive social-relational emotion evoked by a sudden intensification of communal sharing.
Typical signs: warmth in the chest, moist eyes/tears, chills/goosebumps, choked up, buoyancy; motivates devotion and moral commitment to communal bonds.
The five facets correlated highly in every sample despite cultural variation.
practical_applications: Design 'heart-warming' beats around a sudden closeness (reunion, unexpected kindness, being included); the emotion transfers across cultures, the specific signals are local (use Thai relational cues).
limitations: Self-report; online-first 2018 version read; published 2019 Emotion 19(3).

title: Aesthetic experiences and their transformative power: a systematic review
authors: Pizzolante, M., Pelowski, M., et al.
key_findings: 23 included articles (12 theoretical, 11 empirical; 13 empirical studies).
Facilitators: empathy, aesthetic sensitivity, openness, expectations, contextual design; process: cognitive discrepancy, emotion, insight; after-effects: self-change, empathy, critical thinking.
Quality: Downs & Black mean 16.2/27; only two studies had active controls; mostly self-report, uncontrolled designs, rare long-term follow-up.
practical_applications: Claims that a post/clip 'changes lives' are not evidence-based; aim for insight moments and measure modest outcomes (saves, comments).
limitations: Authors' strong conclusion exceeds the evidence quality they report; first half of the text read in detail.

title: Small sample sizes reduce the replicability of task-based fMRI studies
authors: Turner, B. O., et al.
key_findings: Resampling 11 tasks: at typical N about 30, replicability of group maps is modest; smallest N with average R-squared > .5 was 36.
Even at N = 121 the conservative voxel Jaccard overlap stays below 0.6; peaks often fail to replicate.
Good test-retest reliability does not guarantee replicability; recommend power analysis, individual-difference approaches and large studies.
practical_applications: Most neuroaesthetics fMRI studies (N 15-30) should be read as hypothesis-generating; never use them as proof in content claims.
limitations: General fMRI, not aesthetics-specific; authors decline a universal minimum N.
